implementation_notes: The classic C++ realization: the inherited C macro for runtime invariants and the C++11 static_assert keyword for compile-time ones. assert(E) is a constant subexpression when NDEBUG is defined or when the condition is a constant true, so enabled debug runs pay the check and release builds pay nothing. The object-oriented alternative - an invariant() member called by every mutator - is the structure Boost.Contract exists to support; without such a library, keep the predicate as a small const member function asserted after each mutation.
pitfalls: NDEBUG disables assert at the preprocessor level: the expression is not compiled at all, so side effects inside it disappear from release builds.
Because assert is a macro, template arguments containing commas must be parenthesised: assert((std::is_same_v<A, B>)).
Do not assert on public-API argument values: if a caller can supply the bad value, throw instead, otherwise the release build silently accepts the invalid call.
An assertion firing inside a destructor during stack unwinding terminates the program; keep checks out of noexcept cleanup paths.

variants.name: C++26 language-level contract assertions
variants.implementation_notes: C++26 puts contracts into the language: pre and post clauses on functions plus contract_assert statements in bodies replace the macro, and the build selects a violation handler (ignore, observe, enforce or quick-enforce) instead of a single NDEBUG switch. Choose it when the toolchain is C++26 and the contract should be visible in the function declaration; unlike the macro it can keep checking in release builds.
pitfalls: The semantics of a violation depend on the compiler's contract build level: the same code may abort, throw or be ignored across build configurations.
Contracts are not enabled by default in every toolchain; a project must set the contract level explicitly to get the checking it assumes.

variants.name: Boost.Contract library (Eiffel-style pre/post/invariants)
variants.implementation_notes: The library realization for projects that want the whole Eiffel model before C++26: boost::contract::check takes functors for preconditions, postconditions (including old values) and a public invariant() member checked on entry and exit of every public function, with a customizable failure handler. Choose it over the macro when postconditions with old values, class invariants or subcontracting are worth the boilerplate and the runtime dependency.
pitfalls: The macro form needs C++11 lambdas to stay readable; without them the boilerplate functors are worse than the manual checks.
Contracts are compiled into the code and checked at run time like any other library call: the cost is real unless the library's disable macros are set for release builds.
